chapters.title: Chapter 5: Trading Mechanics, Risk and Tax

lessons.title: Leverage and Margin: Why Small Moves Create Big Losses

children.text: On 15 January 2015, the Swiss National Bank scrapped the cap it had kept on the Swiss franc for over three years. Within minutes the franc surged by as much as 30% against the euro, and by some measures more. Thousands of retail traders around the world who had bet against the franc with high leverage did not just lose their deposits. Many ended up owing their brokers money. One UK broker, Alpari UK, became insolvent, and US broker FXCM needed a $300 million rescue after clients ran up about $225 million in negative balances. The currency move was extreme, but the mechanism that turned it into ruin is the same one at work on every leveraged trade. This lesson shows you exactly how leverage and margin turn small currency moves into large gains and, far more often, large losses.

body.text: Leverage does not change how much a currency moves. It changes how much of your money each move puts at risk. Currencies usually move less than 1% a day, which is exactly why they are traded with leverage, and exactly why leveraged traders get wiped out by moves that look tiny on a chart.

children.text: What Leverage Actually Is

markDefs.definition: Controlling a position worth much more than the money you put up. Measured as position value divided by margin.
A demand from your broker to add funds because losses have pushed your account below the required margin.
The point at which a broker automatically closes your positions because your remaining margin has fallen below a set level.

children.text: When you post ₹66,468 of margin to control a EUR/USD futures position worth ₹22,15,600, you are using
leverage
. Gains and losses are calculated on the full ₹22,15,600, but they come out of your ₹66,468. If losses eat into that deposit, your broker sends a
margin call
. On many offshore platforms, the software skips the call and triggers a
stop-out
, closing your trade automatically at whatever price is available.

body.caption: 3% margin means about 33 times leverage; 0.2% margin means 500 times

children.text: Rhea, a Bengaluru software engineer with no currency exposure, uses NSE's cross-currency contracts, which residents may trade without one. She buys 20 lots of EUR/USD futures at 1.1600. That is €20,000, worth $23,200, or ₹22,15,600 at USD/INR 95.50. Her broker blocks margin of 3%, which is ₹66,468.

body.title: Rhea's leverage
body.prompt: Rhea's EUR/USD position is worth ₹22,15,600 and her margin is ₹66,468. What is her leverage? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Leverage = ₹22,15,600 ÷ ₹66,468 = 33.33 times. A 3% margin always gives about 33 times leverage, because 1 ÷ 0.03 = 33.33. Every 1% move in EUR/USD changes her margin by about 33%.

children.text: At 500 times leverage, the bar stops at 100% only because you cannot lose more than everything in the account, at least in theory. In reality, a 1% move at 500x is a loss of five times the deposit, and on a platform without negative balance protection, that shortfall can become a debt. The trader was wiped out after a move of just 0.2%.

body.title: A normal bad day
body.prompt: EUR/USD falls from 1.1600 to 1.1520 against Rhea's 20-lot long position. With the loss converted at USD/INR 95.50, how many rupees does she lose?
body.explanation: Move = 1.1600 minus 1.1520 = 0.0080, or 80 pips. Loss = 0.0080 × €20,000 = $160. In rupees: $160 × 95.50 = ₹15,280. EUR/USD fell only about 0.69%, but Rhea lost about 23% of her ₹66,468 margin in one move.

children.text: The Maths of Getting Back to Zero

Losses and gains are not symmetrical. If your account falls 50%, a 50% gain does not get you back. You need 100%, because the gain is calculated on a smaller base. Leverage makes large drawdowns common, and large drawdowns are brutally hard to recover from.

body.caption: Gain needed to recover from a loss
With the loss written as a decimal, for example 0.50 for a 50% loss

body.title: Climbing back
body.prompt: After a string of leveraged trades, Rhea's trading account is down 40%. What percentage gain does she need on the remaining balance just to get back to where she started? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Gain needed = 0.40 ÷ (1 minus 0.40) = 0.40 ÷ 0.60 = 0.6667, or 66.67%. If she started with ₹1,00,000, she now has ₹60,000 and needs to make ₹40,000 on it, which is 66.67%.

children.text: SEBI's studies cover equity futures and options, not currencies, but the lesson carries over directly: leveraged derivatives in the hands of individuals lose money far more often than they make it. European and UK regulators reached the same conclusion about retail forex and CFD trading and capped leverage on major currency pairs at 30 to 1, far below the 1:500 that offshore apps advertise to Indians.
When Stop-Losses Fail: Gaps

body.title: Why a stop-loss is not a guarantee

markDefs.definition: When the price jumps from one level to another with no trades in between, often after news, a weekend or a policy announcement.
The difference between the price at which you wanted to exit and the price you actually got.

children.text: A stop-loss order becomes a market order once the price reaches your level. If the market
gaps
past that level, your order fills at the next available price, which can be far worse. That difference is
slippage
. In the Swiss franc shock, many stop-loss orders were filled hundreds of pips away from where they were set, because there were simply no buyers at the intermediate prices.

Rupee markets gap too. Weekend news, an overnight US data surprise or an RBI announcement can open USD/INR well away from Friday's close, as the March and April 2026 episode showed. Lower leverage is the only reliable protection against gaps, because it keeps a gap-sized loss survivable.

events.title: Stops fail

body.text: Leverage means something different for a hedger. When Karthik holds EUR/INR futures against a real euro payment, a loss on the futures is matched by a cheaper payment, so his business is not exposed to the leverage the way Rhea's account is. His risk is cash flow: he must be able to pay daily MTM debits. For someone with no underlying exposure, leverage is pure risk, with nothing on the other side to offset it.

Offshore apps market 1:500 or 1:1000 leverage as a feature. It is the opposite. At 500x, a 0.2% move, smaller than a normal day in EUR/USD, wipes out the deposit, and many platforms auto-close positions at 50% margin, which means a 0.1% move. These apps are also not a legal route for Indian residents under FEMA. Leverage that high is designed to transfer deposits from traders to the platform, not to help anyone manage risk.

body.title: The real risk of 1:500
body.question: Aman deposits ₹50,000 on an offshore app and opens a position at 1:500 leverage. Roughly how large an adverse move wipes out his entire deposit?
body.explanation: At 500x leverage, his ₹50,000 controls a position of ₹2.5 crore. A 0.2% move on ₹2.5 crore is ₹50,000, his entire deposit. EUR/USD often moves more than that in a single day.

body.title: Choosing how much leverage to use
body.scenario: Rhea has ₹3,00,000 set aside for learning to trade EUR/USD futures on NSE. Each lot needs about ₹3,323 of margin at a 3% requirement. A friend says: "Your broker allows up to 90 lots with that money. Go big, the margin is just sitting there." Rhea has noticed that EUR/USD commonly moves 0.5% in a day and occasionally 1.5% or more in a week.
body.prompt: Compare using 90 lots with using 10 lots. For each, estimate the rupee loss from a 1.5% adverse move at USD/INR 95.50, express it as a share of her ₹3,00,000, and recommend how she should size positions.
body.modelAnswer:
1. One lot is €1,000, worth about $1,160 at 1.1600, or about ₹1,10,780.
2. With 90 lots, the position is about ₹99.7 lakh, roughly 33 times her ₹3,00,000. A 1.5% adverse move loses about ₹1,49,553, about half her capital in a week.
3. With 10 lots, the position is about ₹11.08 lakh, roughly 3.7 times her capital. The same 1.5% move loses about ₹16,617, about 5.5% of her capital.
4. The margin is not "sitting there" to be used. It is the buffer that keeps her from being forced out by normal volatility. Using all of it means one bad week could halve her account, and she would then need a 100% gain to recover.
5. Recommendation: size positions so that a realistic bad move costs a small, pre-decided share of capital, such as 1% to 2% per trade, and keep most of the account as free cash. Leverage available is not leverage advisable.

body.title: Leverage rules before any leveraged currency trade
steps: Calculate your true leverage: total position value divided by total account capital, not just margin.
Work out the rupee loss from a normal bad day and a bad week before entering.
Keep free cash well beyond the blocked margin for MTM debits.
Assume stop-losses can slip in gaps, around news and on Monday opens.
Never trade on any platform offering leverage in the hundreds; it is both illegal for residents and designed to fail.
If you have a genuine exposure, size the hedge to the exposure, not to the margin you can afford.

body.title: Leverage from margin
body.textWithBlank: A margin requirement of 2% gives leverage of ___ times.
body.explanation: Leverage = 1 ÷ margin = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 times. At 50x, a 2% adverse move wipes out the margin.

cards.definition: Position value divided by margin. 3% margin is about 33x; 0.2% margin is 500x.
A demand to add funds after losses push your account below required margin.
Automatic closure of positions by a broker when margin falls below a set level.
A jump in price with no trades in between, which can make stop-losses fill far away from their level.
Gain needed = loss ÷ (1 minus loss). A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover.
When losses exceed the deposit, leaving the trader owing money, as many did in the 2015 Swiss franc shock.

points: Leverage is position value divided by margin. It multiplies every currency move by the same factor on your capital.
At 33x, a 1% move changes your margin by about 33%; at 500x, a 0.2% move wipes it out.
Losses are asymmetric: a 50% loss needs a 100% gain just to break even.
SEBI found 93% of individual equity F&O traders lost money over FY22 to FY24, and European regulators capped retail forex leverage at 30 to 1.
Stop-losses can slip badly in gaps, as the 2015 Swiss franc shock showed. Lower leverage is the only reliable defence.
For hedgers, leverage is offset by the underlying exposure; the risk is cash flow. For everyone else, it is pure risk.
Available leverage is not advisable leverage. Size positions by the loss you can accept, not the margin you have.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Margin levels and prices in the examples are illustrative and change with market conditions. Rupee-pair derivatives may be used only to hedge genuine currency exposures; offshore leveraged forex platforms are not a legal route for Indian residents. Leveraged trading can cause losses larger than expected.
